nameStory: The Smooth-footed Powderhorn gets its name from its unique combination of features - the 'smooth foot' refers to the clean, unbranched base of its upright structures, while 'powderhorn' describes the curved, hollow tubes that resemble the powder horns once used to store gunpowder. Unlike many of its Cladonia cousins that have scaly or branched bases, this lichen keeps things neat and tidy at ground level.
description: Smooth-footed Powderhorn is a small, cup-and-goblet style lichen that creates miniature landscapes on rotting wood and soil. It produces tiny, curved trumpet-like structures that stand about half an inch tall, often with a subtle yellowish-green tint. The base consists of small, grayish-green scales that lie flat against the surface, from which the smooth-stemmed 'horns' emerge. This delicate lichen forms small colonies that look like tiny musical instruments scattered across decaying logs.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Small curved tubes or narrow funnels rising from flat, scaly bases - feel smooth and papery when dry, like delicate parchment

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale yellowish-green to gray-green when dry, becoming more vibrant green when moist - the color change is quite dramatic after rain

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, clean stems without the powdery coating found on many similar species - run your finger along them and they feel surprisingly sleek

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny structures typically 0.5-1 inch tall, with trumpet openings about the size of a pencil eraser

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on well-rotted, soft wood that crumbles easily when touched - rarely on soil or rock

habitat: Look for Smooth-footed Powderhorn on very decayed logs and stumps in moist, shaded areas of New England's mixed and coniferous forests. It prefers wood that's in advanced stages of decomposition - the kind that's soft enough to poke your finger into. You'll often find it in company with mosses and other small cup lichens in these quiet, humid forest corners.

seasonality.spring: Most visible after spring rains when the pale structures turn a vibrant green and stand out clearly against dark, wet wood. New growth may be emerging from the basal scales.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen becomes pale and papery, easily overlooked among other forest debris. Look closely in shaded areas where some moisture persists.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture brings back the green coloration, and the lichen is often easiest to spot against newly fallen leaves that haven't yet covered the logs.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round but often muted in color. Snow cover may hide specimens, but they remain active underneath and can be found on exposed log surfaces.

funFact: Despite being called a 'smooth-footed' lichen, this species actually has no feet at all - it's a fungus partnered with algae, and what looks like a 'foot' is actually the fungal body creating a platform to launch its reproductive spores as high as possible into the air currents!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Common Powderhorn, but the Common species has a distinctly powdery, granular coating on its stems that rubs off on your fingers - think of it as 'smooth versus sandpapery' when you gently touch the tubes. The Smooth-footed also tends to be more curved and irregular in shape.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'ochrochlora' combines Greek words meaning 'pale yellow' and 'green,' perfectly describing this lichen's subtle color variations. Despite its specific name, this species can be quite variable in color, leading to identification challenges even among experienced lichenologists.
compareHints: Among the powderhorn group of Cladonia lichens, Smooth-footed stands out for its clean, uncoated stems and preference for very rotten wood. While Lipstick Powderhorn has bright red tips and Common Powderhorn has that telltale granular coating, Smooth-footed keeps things simple with its sleek, curved tubes and muted colors. It's also typically smaller and more delicate than its powderhorn relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: British soldier lichen differs from its Cladonia relatives by having consistently red-topped reproductive structures rather than brown or yellow ones.
Star-tipped Reindeer Lichen stands out from its Cladonia cousins by forming the most distinctly cushion-shaped colonies with the densest branching pattern.
Gray reindeer lichen differs from other Cladonia species by its consistently gray color and terrestrial growth habit - most pixie cup lichens are smaller and many grow on rotting wood.
Among all the Cladonia species in New England, fishnet cladonia is unique for its wide, perforated stalks - no other pixie cup or reindeer lichen has this Swiss cheese appearance.
Common Powderhorn differs from its pixie cup relatives by its consistently powdery, granular surface texture - Pebbled Pixie Cup is much bumpier, while Mealy Pixie Cup is smoother.

Giant Cladonia stands apart from its genus relatives primarily through sheer size—while British Soldier lichens top out around 2 inches and most reindeer lichens form low, branching mats, Giant Cladonia towers above them all.
Unlike the bright red caps of British Soldier lichen or the branched, coral-like growth of reindeer lichens, Dragon Horn has a unique two-tier structure with scaly bases and pointed projections.
Green Reindeer Lichen differs from Gray Reindeer Lichen mainly in color (more greenish tints when wet) and slightly more complex branching patterns.
Unlike British Soldier lichen with its bright red caps on straight stalks, Red-fruited Pixie Cup has an actual cup or goblet shape with red fruiting bodies around the rim.

Many-forked cladonia branches more frequently and regularly than most of its Cladonia relatives—while British soldiers have simple stalks topped with red caps, and reindeer lichens have more irregular branching, many-forked cladonia creates dense networks of repeated Y-shaped forks.
Unlike pixie cup lichens that form neat goblet shapes, Thorn Lichen branches end in sharp points.
Dixie Reindeer Lichen is distinguished from other Cladonia species by its consistently small size and extremely fine, dense branching pattern.
Unlike its cousin the British Soldier Lichen which has bright red caps on shorter, more robust stalks, Lipstick Powderhorn has taller, more slender trumpet-shaped stalks.
Among its Cladonia relatives, trumpet lichen's fringed cup edges help distinguish it from the smoother Pebbled Pixie Cup and the bright red-capped British Soldier lichen.
Powder-foot British Soldiers differs from regular British Soldier lichen by its distinctive white powdery base coating on the stalks.
Unlike the bright red caps of British Soldier Lichen or the dense, spongy masses of Reindeer Lichens, Ladder Lichen has a more delicate, architectural appearance.
Compared to its close relative Gray Reindeer Lichen, Dune Reindeer Lichen is much smaller and more delicate, forming low cushions rather than tall, prominent clumps.
Unlike the smooth, waxy Pebbled Pixie Cup or the bright red-capped British Soldier lichen, Mealy Pixie Cup is distinguished by its powdery, dusty coating and consistently pale coloration.
Unlike the tall, elegant cups of Trumpet Lichen or the branching antler-like forms of reindeer lichens, Stubby-stalked Cladonia keeps a low profile with its characteristic short stalks.
Unlike cup-forming cladonias such as pixie cups or powderhorns, fence-rail cladonia lacks the distinctive cup or funnel shapes at branch tips.
Unlike its smooth-surfaced cousin the Mealy Pixie Cup, this species has that distinctive gritty texture.
Unlike the branched antler-like structures of reindeer lichens or the cup-shaped forms of pixie cup lichens, Smooth Horn Lichen produces simple, unbranched tubes.
Gritty British soldiers differs from regular British soldier lichen by its distinctly rough, gritty stalk texture and lack of powdery soredia.
Unlike the wider cups of Pebbled Pixie Cup or the branched trumpets of Trumpet Lichen, Quill Lichen produces distinctively narrow, unbranched tubes.
Unlike the British Soldier lichens with their bright red caps, or the Pebbled Pixie Cups with their eventual tall stalks, Stalkless Cladonia stays perpetually low and cup-shaped.

Among the many Cladonia species in New England, Olive Cladonia stands out for its distinctive olive-green coloration - most other cup lichens are gray-green (like Mealy Pixie Cup) or have bright red tips (like British Soldier Lichen).
Among its Cladonia relatives, Mealy Forked Cladonia stands out for its powdery coating - most other forked species like Many-forked Cladonia have smooth surfaces.
Unlike British soldier lichen with its bright red caps or the branching patterns of reindeer lichens, wand lichen maintains simple, unbranched points.
